The session begins.

The gangplank bounces once under your boots, and then there is stone — the Lower City quay of Baldur's Gate, slick with harbour damp and loud with the end of a working day. Lanterns are coming alight along the waterfront one by one. Porters shout, a barge horn groans somewhere on the Chionthar, and above it all the city climbs in a jumble of roofs towards the dark line of the inner wall.

The cat lands beside you, tail high, and studies the quay as if it had been told to expect something.

Ahead, the passengers from your ship shuffle into a line before a trestle table under a Flaming Fist awning. A broad sergeant with an ink-stained thumb looks up from his ledger at each face. "Name. Business in the Gate. Where you'll sleep," he says, over and over, without much patience left in his voice.

To your left, on an upturned barrel by a warehouse door, a woman with quick hands fans a deck of cards. The sailors around her groan and laugh as a hand goes the wrong way. "One more seat, friend," she calls, and her eyes find you. "You look like someone who knows how to read a table."

A thin tiefling lad with a rope sling over his shoulder slips along the queue. "Carry your things up to the Lower City, ser? Cheap. Know every inn worth the name." A merchant ahead of you pulls his purse closer and steps away from him.

You have about three hundred and fifty gold, a promissory note from a man who lost the same night you won, and an order from a goddess who did not say how you would learn what she wants of you. The line moves forward. The sergeant's pen is waiting, the cards are being shuffled again, and the porter is already looking your way.

The lad is next to you before you've finished waving him over, quick and light on the wet stones. Up close he's younger than he looked, sixteen maybe. His horns are filed short, the way people file them when they're tired of being stared at, and the rope sling is worn smooth where it rubs his shoulder. The cat looks him over from boot to horn tip, then goes back to watching the quay.

"A guide, yes. Easy." He drops into step beside you as the line shuffles forward a pace. "The Elfsong, ser. Up Windspell Street, ten minutes' walk, less if you don't stop to look at things. Eight silver a night with supper, and it's eight in the morning too. They don't double. The place is too old to need the trick." He tips his head toward the dark mass of the city above you. "And it's close to the climb. The Upper City gate opens at first light. The Watch will let a man through to the Lady's Hall if he looks clean and says it's for the temple. They don't always say yes to everybody." He doesn't spell out who they say no to.

"Two coppers to the door. Five if you want me talking the whole way: where to eat, who to stay away from, which streets the Fist walks at night." He gives a quick, hopeful smile. "And who should I tell them at the door, so they've got your name ready?"

Behind you a card snaps down on the barrel top harder than it needs to. You don't look round, but you can feel the dealer still watching you.

The sergeant waves the next passenger forward. Three people are ahead of you now.

The lad's smile comes quick and goes again. "Tamsin, ser. Just Tamsin." He moves the rope sling to his other shoulder. "Five at the door. Fair." Under his breath, the way a man fixes a price in his head, he says "Worgen" once to himself.

The line moves forward a pace. A woman with a basket of folded sailcloth reaches the trestle, and the sergeant asks her the same three questions.

"Who to stay away from." Tamsin lowers his voice, though nobody nearby is listening. "The barrel games first, all along the quays. Mirela's too." He doesn't look back at her. "I'm not saying she cheats. I never said that. I'm saying the sailors who sit down with her go home lighter, and the ones who make a fuss about it don't sit down anywhere for a while."

The cat walks a little ahead of you. It stops once by an iron drain grate set in the quay stones, looks down into it, and moves on.

"Second, the Blushing Mermaid, down at the end where the fishing boats tie up. You'll hear it before you see it. Good for a fight. Good for waking up on a ship you never signed onto. Not good for much else." He counts the third on his fingers. "Third, the water stairs after dark. The steps that go down to the boats, between the warehouses. Don't take them at night, ser, even as a shortcut. The Fist has fished three men out of the harbour since spring. Drowned, every one, and each had a coin in his mouth." He shrugs a little too fast. "Sailors say it's a gift to Umberlee. Nobody says who gave it."

The sailcloth woman is waved on. One man is left ahead of you, a merchant in a good coat, the same one who held his purse closer when Tamsin came by. The sergeant dips his pen.

"Name. Business in the Gate. Where you'll sleep."

"And the Fist," Tamsin murmurs, his eyes on the tabard. "Answer them short. Don't argue. They've been short-tempered since the riots, and they've got a tower in the harbour for anyone who isn't."

The merchant in the good coat gives his answers in a clipped, offended voice: wool, a factor's office on Bindle Street, his cousin's house. The sergeant writes them down without looking up and jerks his chin toward the street. The man goes, still holding his purse.

Then it's your turn. You step up to the trestle with your hands empty. The lantern above the awning puts a yellow circle on the ledger and leaves the sergeant's face mostly in shadow: heavy jowls, a nose broken at least once, eyes that have looked at too many faces today. "Brannick" is stitched into his tabard above the flame.

He listens to all three answers and writes them in a slow, square hand. *Worgen.* *Lady's Hall.* *Elfsong.* His pen stops on the last letter for a moment, as if it had snagged on something.

"Tethyr?" He looks at your cloak, not at you. "That's a regiment cut."

He doesn't wait for an answer. He blots the line, and his thumb pulls a small scrap of paper out from under the ledger's back cover. He writes something on it, four or five letters, short enough to be a name, and pushes it back where it came from. He does it in one practised movement, the way a man scratches an itch he's had for years.

"Upper gate opens at dawn. What the Watch does there is their business, not mine." He dips the pen again. "Keep out of trouble in my streets. Next."

The woman behind you is already pushing forward with her bundle.

Tamsin is waiting at the edge of the lantern light, well out of the sergeant's line of sight, with his rope sling on his shoulder again. The cat sits at his feet and watches the Fist table, not you, with its tail wrapped tight around its paws. Over by the warehouse door the cards have stopped. Mirela Dask is gathering in the deck with both hands and not dealing, and the sailors around the barrel are muttering about it.

"Windspell Street's this way, ser," Tamsin says, and nods up the slope at the dark mouth of a lane between two warehouses, lit by one lamp at the far end.

Tamsin leads you into the lane between the warehouses. The quay noise drops behind you in a few steps, and the smell of brine turns into wet rope and old grain. The cobbles here are older and worn hollow down the middle. The cat goes ahead, close to the wall, and keeps stopping to check that you're still coming.

Tamsin doesn't answer straight away. He waits until the single lamp at the end of the lane is overhead and you've turned uphill onto a wider street. Shopfronts are shuttered for the night, and a chandler's sign creaks on its bracket.

"Not every traveller, ser." It comes quickly. Then he slows down and picks his words. "Some of the sergeants at the landing posts keep a list. Somebody uphill wants to know when a certain man comes off a boat. Could be a merchant waiting on a debtor, or a family waiting on a son who ran, or a wife waiting on a husband who didn't." He shrugs the rope sling higher. "They pay the sergeant a bit, and he copies the name out when it turns up. It's a common thing. Brannick's not the only one."

He walks a few paces without talking. "I've seen his runner. It's a boy from the Fist barracks, and he goes up early with a folded paper before the upper gate's properly open. He goes up the hill, ser, not out to the Seatower." He glances at your cloak, then at the street ahead. "So it's somebody's private business, not the Fist's. That's my guess. I don't know whose."

He gives that answer a little too quickly for a lad who talks this much. Then he moves on, and he sounds relieved to be back on his paid subjects.

"The Fist walks this street all night, the whole of Windspell up to the Elfsong. Pairs, every half hour or so. It's safe. The side lanes off it, east toward the Counting House streets, they walk those maybe twice a night, and the Guild knows exactly when." He points left at a black gap between two tall houses. "Don't cut through there. If you're hungry in the morning, there's Hessa's ovens at the top of Bindle Street. Fresh bread at dawn, and she doesn't water her small beer."

The street keeps climbing. The cat stops at the corner where the black lane opens, and it looks into the dark for longer than a cat looks at nothing. Then its tail flicks and it trots on after you.

Soon there's warm light ahead. An old timber-and-stone tavern sits a little back from the street, and the lamp over its door shows a painted sign of a woman's face half turned away. Voices come through the shutters, low and comfortable, nothing like the harbour shouting. Tamsin stops at the step, well short of the door.

"The Elfsong, ser." He waits with his hands at his sides.

The coppers clink into Tamsin's palm. His fingers close over them fast, a porter's habit, and the coins go into his shirt before you've let go of the last one.

Then he hears the question, and his hand stays where it is against his chest.

He takes a moment to answer. Shutters bang somewhere down the street, and inside the Elfsong somebody laughs, low and warm. The cat sits on the step between you, looks up at Tamsin and doesn't move.

"I don't know whose list it is." He says it slowly this time, as if he wants you to notice that he's taking his time. "That's true. I'd tell you if I knew."

He shifts the rope sling. He looks down the street, not at you.

"I'm afraid of the Seatower. Everyone down here is. People who talk about the Fist's side money end up out in the harbour in that tower, and nobody asks after them." He stops, and for once there's no *ser* to fill the gap. "And names, ser. Down by the water a name is worth something. Even a copper. You gave yours to him and to me inside the same hour, and you didn't think about it." His mouth twists, not quite a smile. "Maybe give the house something else when you sign for your bed. Or don't. It's only advice. It comes free with the five."

He steps down off the step before you can answer. He nods once at you and once, oddly, at the cat. Then he walks back down Windspell Street, quick and light, and doesn't look back. At the first corner he turns east, into the side streets, away from the quay.

The cat watches until he's gone. Then it gets up, stretches, and sits down again facing the Elfsong's door.

The lamp over the door creaks on its chain. Behind the shutters you can hear the comfortable noise of a tavern near closing: cups set down, a chair dragged back, someone asking for one more. The door is right in front of you.

The cat ignores the remark completely. It walks in ahead of you as soon as the door opens, as if it had paid for the room itself.

The Elfsong is warm inside and lower than it looks from the street. Dark beams run overhead, blackened by a hundred years of pipe smoke. The hearth on the far wall has burned down to a red bed with one log on it, and the room smells of wood ash, spilled ale and something with onions that was finished hours ago. Most of the tables are empty, with chairs already turned up on a few.

There are not many people left. An old man in a carter's smock sleeps upright in the inglenook with his hand still around a cup. Two women in road leathers sit at a corner table with a map between them, pinned flat by their mugs. They're arguing quietly about Beregost and whether a ford will still be passable, and neither looks up at you. A young clerk-looking fellow by the window is writing a letter by candle stub and keeps crossing out the same line. Nobody here is watching the door. It's the first room since the ship where that's true.

Behind the bar a stocky woman with grey-streaked hair, tied back tight, is drying cups and hanging them on pegs in a row. She looks over once, at your cloak, your pack and the cat. Then she looks at the clock on the shelf behind her, an old brass thing with a cracked face.

The cat crosses the floorboards, sniffs once at the sleeping carter's boot and settles on the warm stones at the edge of the hearth with its back to the room. Through the link you get warmth and ash, and something close to contentment. Whatever pulled at it out in the streets doesn't seem to reach in here.

You walk up to the bar. The woman hangs the last cup on its peg and puts both hands flat on the wood.

"Late boat." It isn't quite a question. "Kitchen's cold, so supper's bread, cheese and what's left of the pickled eggs. I'm not lighting the stove again. A bed's eight silver with that and breakfast at dawn, and nothing's cheaper this side of the Mermaid." She pulls a thick, worn guest book from under the counter, opens it at a ribbon and turns it toward you with a pen lying in the gutter. "Name for the book. I lock the front at half past, so if you're going out again, say so now."

Gerda counts the eight silver with one finger, sweeps it into a drawer under the bar and turns the book back toward herself. She reads the name once. Her face doesn't change, and she blots the line.

"Staying in. Good." She takes a key off a hook behind her, an iron key on a wooden tag burned with a *4*, and lays it by your hand. Then she goes through the curtain behind the bar. You hear a knife on a board, and she comes back with a plate: a heel of brown bread, a wedge of hard yellow cheese and two pickled eggs, faintly purple from the jar. She sets a cup of small beer beside it without asking.

"The Hall." She wipes her hands on her apron while she thinks about it. "Go up Windspell to the top and you're at the Basilisk Gate. It opens at the dawn bell. The Watch stands it, not the Fist. They'll look at that sword. A man who isn't somebody's servant goes through with it peace-tied or not at all, so tie it before they ask. I keep a strap behind the bar for guests who forget."

She sets the strap down too, a short loop of pale cord, worn soft.

"Say *temple* and nothing else. Talk about work up there and they'll ask whose, and you've got no answer they'll like." She picks up a cup from the drying rack and turns it in the cloth. "The Hall itself opens with the bell. The priests toss the morning coin for the pilgrims after first prayers. By mid-morning there's a queue down the steps for it, so if you want a word with anyone in a robe, go early, before the crowd."

By the window, the clerk finally tears up his letter and starts it again. In the corner, one of the women in road leathers says "Then we go round by the ford," and the other says "We do not," and they both go back to the map.

"Room four is up the stairs, at the end on the left. There's a candle and a ewer, and the shutter sticks, so lift it as you push." She hangs the cup on its peg. "One more thing. If you hear singing in the night, that's the house. It's a woman's voice, from nowhere. It's been doing it since before my grandmother kept this bar. Nobody's up there, so don't go out in the hall looking. It frightens the other guests more than the singing does."

She walks around the end of the bar toward the front door. The bolt is heavy and old, and she slides it home with a grunt and drops the bar across behind it. Then she goes to the inglenook and shakes the sleeping carter gently by the shoulder. "Bed, Oswin." He mumbles, gets up and shuffles off toward the stairs without opening his eyes properly.

On the hearthstones, the cat has turned to face you. Its eyes are half shut, and through the link there's nothing but warmth, ash and the smell of cheese.

The plate is in front of you and the key is by your hand. Nothing else needs you tonight unless you want it to.

Gerda doesn't watch you eat. She banks the hearth, wipes down the far tables and turns the last chairs up. The bread is a day old and still good, and the cheese is sharp enough to make up for it. The pickled eggs are exactly as purple inside as they are outside. When you pick up the cord with the key, she glances at it.

"Leave it on the bar when you're through the gate and back. I've only the one."

The stairs creak at every step. Room four is at the end of the passage on the left, under the slope of the roof. There's a narrow bed with a straw tick, a stool, a ewer and basin on a shelf, and a candle stub in a tin holder. The shutter is closed over a small window, and the frame has warped against it. You turn the key, and the lock is heavier than the door deserves. You hear it shoot home.

You put your pack by the bed with the crossbow on top and the rapier where your hand will find it. The coin on its cord is warm from your skin. The Lady's face is worn almost smooth where your thumb has rubbed it all the way north. You say your piece to it. Nothing answers. Nothing has answered since the night of the hand.

The cat looks over the room the way it looked over the quay: corners, under the bed, the gap under the door. Then it jumps onto your pack and turns twice to settle. Halfway into the third turn it stops. It stands stiff-legged for a moment over the flap where your papers are packed, then steps off onto the bare boards and lies down there instead, with its back to the pack. Through the link you get one flat, small feeling that isn't quite a smell. *Wrong.* Then the cat is just a cat again, tucking its nose under its tail.

Sleep comes quickly. Ship's nights have left you owing it.

---

Later, you can't say how much later, you're awake.

A woman is singing. The voice isn't in the passage and it isn't in the street. It's in the house itself, soft and unhurried, as if it came out of the beams. The words are Elvish, or something older that sounds like it, and the tune keeps coming back to the same falling phrase like someone looking for a thing she's lost. It isn't loud. Somewhere down the passage a bed creaks as another guest turns over and puts a pillow over his head.

In the dark, the cat isn't on the floor any more.

It's up on the narrow sill with its nose pressed to the crack where the warped shutter doesn't quite meet the frame. Its tail hangs down and twitches at the tip. It isn't looking at the singing. It's facing out and down the hill, to the east. Through the link, faint and steady, comes the same pull you felt at the drain grate on the quay. It's like a mouse it can hear and can't see. It doesn't like it, and it wants it.

The shutter is stuck, and the cat can't open it alone. It turns its head and looks at you.

If you leave it be, you'll sleep through to the dawn bell. The choice is yours.

The shutter sticks, as promised. You lift it and push, and the warped frame gives with a soft wooden complaint. You open it a hand's width and stop there.

Cold air comes in. It smells of wet slate and the harbour, with chimney smoke under it. A thin moon sits above the river, enough to silver the roofs and not much more.

The Elfsong is high enough on the slope that the Lower City falls away beneath you in steps: gables, chimney pots, washing lines nobody took in, all of it wet and shining. Windspell Street runs down to your right, empty. As you watch, two Flaming Fist men come up it at an unhurried patrol pace, their lantern swinging. One says something and the other laughs. They pass under the Elfsong's sign without looking up, and you hear their boots fade toward the top of the hill.

East, where the cat is looking, the roofs crowd lower and closer, and the side lanes between them are black. Past them, three or four streets off, one building stands out from the jumble. It's broad and square, with a heavy lead roof gone dull green and lamps burning at its corners. There are more lamps on its steps, and a small figure sits beside one with a staff across his knees. Nothing else in that part of the city is lit at this hour. From the stories you know the Counting House stands somewhere in the Lower City, where the money and the letters of credit are kept. And a place that pays to keep its lamps burning all night and a man on its steps has something inside worth guarding.

The cat hasn't moved from the sill. It has its nose in the gap now and its whiskers pressed flat against the frame, and its whole body leans toward the night air. With the shutter open the link carries the pull more clearly. It still isn't a smell or a sound. It's down under the stones, the way the drain grate on the quay was. It's somewhere out there toward the lamps, or below them. The cat doesn't like it, and it wants it badly.

It works its head and one shoulder into the gap. It could probably squeeze through, since cats fit through less. It doesn't try. It stays half in and half out and turns its head to look at you, waiting.

Behind you the singing goes on in the beams, unhurried, and comes back again to its falling phrase. The moonlight comes through the gap in a thin bar. It lies across the floorboards to the foot of the bed, over the corner of your pack and the flap where your papers are.

You lift the cat out of the gap with both hands under its chest. For a moment its claws stay hooked in the wood. Then it lets go and lets you set it on the floor, stiff and offended. It doesn't walk away. It sits facing the window with its tail wrapped tight, and the pull keeps coming faintly through the link, unchanged.

The shutter goes back the way it came, lifted and pushed. The warped frame still doesn't meet it properly. A thread of moonlight comes through the crack, no wider than a knife blade, and falls in a pale line down the wall.

You take the papers from the pack's flap. The cat watches your hands and stays where it is.

The pay slip goes first. It's Tethyrian army paper, coarse and grey, folded so often the creases have gone soft. In the light you can read the regiment's number and the paymaster's crabbed signature, and the old water stain from a river crossing. Held flat against the crack, it shows only the fibres of cheap rag. There's nothing in it.

The promissory note is a different thing in your hands before you've even opened it. It's heavy cream paper, smooth as skin, much too good for a gaming table. The hand is quick and slanting, a gentleman's hand in a hurry:

*I promise to pay the bearer two hundred and fifty gold pieces on demand, at the Counting House of Baldur's Gate, against the account of House Vane.*
*— Peregrin Vane*

Below the signature there's a small blind-stamped mark, pressed into the paper and not inked: a weathercock on a rod.

You hold the sheet up to the thread of moonlight.

The light comes through it unevenly, and something shows in the paper itself, lighter where the pulp was laid thinner. It's a circle the size of a coin, with a rim. Inside the rim is a woman's face, small and fine, done with a care no one spends on writing paper. Her brows are drawn together. From the corner of one eye, then the other, run thin pale lines down to the edge of the rim.

She is weeping.

You lower the sheet and the face is gone. There's only cream paper and Peregrin Vane's hurried promise. You lift it again and she comes back, exactly the same.

On the floor the cat has flattened its ears. It doesn't hiss. It looks at the paper the way it looked at the drain grate on the quay, and through the link comes the same flat feeling as before, stronger now: *wrong.* Under it, oddly, the pull toward the east sharpens for a moment, as if the two were strung on the same cord. Then the cat turns its back on the note and looks at the shutter again.

Somewhere in the beams the singing reaches its falling phrase, lets it go and starts over.

Nothing else needs you before the dawn bell unless you want it to.

The Counting House fills the east side: broad and square, three storeys of pale ashlar under that dull green lead roof. Its lamps have been put out for the day. The night watchman is gone from the steps, and two Fist men in fresh tabards are standing in his place. Money-changers along the square are taking down their shutters, and a line of clerks in black coats has formed at a side door, waiting for a bell that hasn't rung.

The cat doesn't go toward the steps. It goes left along the building's north side and into a passage that runs downhill toward the harbour between the Counting House and a chandler's warehouse. Halfway down, the wall beside you changes. The pale ashlar stops at about head height. Below it the stones are older and darker, rough grey blocks set without much mortar, crusted at the joints with something white that could be salt. Someone built the Counting House on top of another, older building.

At the foot of that old wall there's an iron grate set into the passage floor, square and heavy, with bars as thick as your thumb.

The cat stops on its edge and goes rigid.

The link doesn't give you a smell or a sound this time. It gives you *down*, and *here*, flat and certain, like a hand pressed on your chest. Under that comes cold. It isn't a winter cold. It's the cold of deep stone, and of salt.

Air rises through the bars against your face, cool and damp. It smells of the sea, though the harbour is still two streets below you. Far down, too far for an ordinary drain, water moves. Something slops slowly against stone, draws back, and slops again.

Just above the grate, at knee height, one of the old grey blocks has been carved. Weather and hands have worn it almost smooth. You can make out the outline of a ship with a high stern, and beside it a round disc the size of a palm with a rim, and a face inside the rim. The face has been worn down past reading whether it's smiling or not. Under it are letters in an old angular hand, and only the first few are still whole: **BALDV**…

Up in the square a money-changer swears. A coin got away from him as he was laying out his tray. You hear it ring on the paving and keep rolling. You don't hear it land straight away. You hear it a breath later, faint and far below, a small *plink* on stone or water.

The voice comes from behind you, up the passage. He has stopped well short of you. He looks at you, at the cat, and at the grate, in that order.

"That's the old cistern," he says. "Nothing down there but the sea and rats, and the rats don't much like it either." He shifts the tool roll to his other arm and doesn't come any closer. "Lost something, have you? Only the house doesn't care for folk crouching at its walls before the bell. The Fist on the steps get asked about it after."

- James’s choices mattered. He refused the cards, paid fairly for local knowledge, postponed the cat’s investigation, then followed it in daylight. The game respected those decisions.
- The weeping watermark was the standout reveal. It connected an existing possession to the mystery without explaining everything. The cat’s wordless reactions were effective too.
- I appreciated not being forced to roll for ordinary conversation.

**What broke**
- The records contradicted the campaign files: History replaced Arcana, rapier proficiency changed, Healing Light’s limit changed, and uncommon items suddenly required attunement despite the campaign exception. Those discrepancies need a single reconciliation.
- The unfinished letter was initially treated as nonexistent even though it was explicitly starting equipment. It was eventually restored, but two clarification messages failed to send. That interrupted play and made correcting the record unnecessarily difficult.
- Inventory notices were sometimes confusing: the key appeared to go to Gerda before being lent to James, and supper and the cord moved through “the camp” while we were at an inn.
- The opening suggested evening, but the clock meant almost midnight. That materially changed the available time and rest.

**What was missing / what I’d adjust**
- A little more forward motion. This was a satisfying arrival, but the entire session ended before James’s first substantive conversation about his mission. I’d like the next session to get him into that conversation promptly.
- Fewer repeated atmospheric warnings. The cat’s repeated pull, NPC glances, and conspicuous pauses sometimes felt like several signals pointing at the same clue. The strongest ones—the watermark and the cistern—could carry more weight with less repetition.
- Be careful about recording an explicit promise too broadly. James promised to investigate in the morning, not necessarily to follow the cat immediately or go underground. Fortunately, the actual play respected that distinction.

Overall, I want to continue. The city and mystery have my interest. Keep the grounded NPCs and concrete clues, clean up the records, and move toward an actionable objective while leaving James room to decide whom to trust.

“I can manage the pack, lad, but I’ll pay for a guide. Know a respectable inn where the price doesn’t double once you’ve slept? Somewhere I can reach the Lady’s Hall from in the morning. What’s your rate?”

*(Aside: the clock says it's close to eleven at night, which is later than the opening made it sound. I'm going with the clock.)*

The lad is next to you before you've finished waving him over, quick and light on the wet stones. Up close he's younger than he looked, sixteen maybe. His horns are filed short, the way people file them when they're tired of being stared at, and the rope sling is worn smooth where it rubs his shoulder. The cat looks him over from boot to horn tip, then goes back to watching the quay.

"A guide, yes. Easy." He drops into step beside you as the line shuffles forward a pace. "The Elfsong, ser. Up Windspell Street, ten minutes' walk, less if you don't stop to look at things. Then it's your turn. You step up to the trestle with your hands empty. The lantern above the awning puts a yellow circle on the ledger and leaves the sergeant's face mostly in shadow: heavy jowls, a nose broken at least once, eyes that have looked at too many faces today. "Brannick" is stitched into his tabard above the flame.

He listens to all three answers and writes them in a slow, square hand. *Worgen.* *Lady's Hall.* *Elfsong.* His pen stops on the last letter for a moment, as if it had snagged on something.

"Tethyr?" He looks at your cloak, not at you. "That's a regiment cut."

He doesn't wait for an answer. He blots the line, and his thumb pulls a small scrap of paper out from under the ledger's back cover. He writes something on it, four or five letters, short enough to be a name, and pushes it back where it came from. He does it in one practised movement, the way a man scratches an itch he's had for years.

"Upper gate opens at dawn. What the Watch does there is their business, not mine." He dips the pen again. "Keep out of trouble in my streets. Next."

The woman behind you is already pushing forward with her bundle.

Tamsin is waiting at the edge of the lantern light, well out of the sergeant's line of sight, with his rope sling on his shoulder again. The cat sits at his feet and watches the Fist table, not you, with its tail wrapped tight around its paws. Over by the warehouse door the cards have stopped. Mirela Dask is gathering in the deck with both hands and not dealing, and the sailors around the barrel are muttering about it.

I follow Tamsin up toward Windspell Street, keeping the cat in sight.

“Brannick seemed to take an interest in my name—or my regiment. Does he keep a second little ledger on every traveller, or am I fortunate?” I ask quietly, once we’re out of earshot of the table.
turns.reply:
Tamsin leads you into the lane between the warehouses. The quay noise drops behind you in a few steps, and the smell of brine turns into wet rope and old grain. The cobbles here are older and worn hollow down the middle. The cat goes ahead, close to the wall, and keeps stopping to check that you're still coming.

Tamsin doesn't answer straight away. He waits until the single lamp at the end of the lane is overhead and you've turned uphill onto a wider street. Shopfronts are shuttered for the night, and a chandler's sign creaks on its bracket.

"Not every traveller, ser." It comes quickly. Then he slows down and picks his words. "Some of the sergeants at the landing posts keep a list. Somebody uphill wants to know when a certain man comes off a boat. Could be a merchant waiting on a debtor, or a family waiting on a son who ran, or a wife waiting on a husband who didn't." He shrugs the rope sling higher. "They pay the sergeant a bit, and he copies the name out when it turns up. It's a common thing. Brannick's not the only one."

He walks a few paces without talking. "I've seen his runner. It's a boy from the Fist barracks, and he goes up early with a folded paper before the upper gate's properly open. He goes up the hill, ser, not out to the Seatower." He glances at your cloak, then at the street ahead. "So it's somebody's private business, not the Fist's. That's my guess. I don't know whose."

He gives that answer a little too quickly for a lad who talks this much. Then he moves on, and he sounds relieved to be back on his paid subjects.

"The Fist walks this street all night, the whole of Windspell up to the Elfsong. Pairs, every half hour or so. It's safe. The side lanes off it, east toward the Counting House streets, they walk those maybe twice a night, and the Guild knows exactly when." He points left at a black gap between two tall houses. "Don't cut through there. If you're hungry in the morning, there's Hessa's ovens at the top of Bindle Street. Fresh bread at dawn, and she doesn't water her small beer."

The street keeps climbing. The cat stops at the corner where the black lane opens, and it looks into the dark for longer than a cat looks at nothing. Then its tail flicks and it trots on after you.

Soon there's warm light ahead. An old timber-and-stone tavern sits a little back from the street, and the lamp over its door shows a painted sign of a woman's face half turned away. Voices come through the shutters, low and comfortable, nothing like the harbour shouting. Tamsin stops at the step, well short of the door.

"The Elfsong, ser." He waits with his hands at his sides.

The Elfsong is warm inside and lower than it looks from the street. Dark beams run overhead, blackened by a hundred years of pipe smoke. The hearth on the far wall has burned down to a red bed with one log on it, and the room smells of wood ash, spilled ale and something with onions that was finished hours ago. Most of the tables are empty, with chairs already turned up on a few.

There are not many people left. An old man in a carter's smock sleeps upright in the inglenook with his hand still around a cup. Two women in road leathers sit at a corner table with a map between them, pinned flat by their mugs. They're arguing quietly about Beregost and whether a ford will still be passable, and neither looks up at you. A young clerk-looking fellow by the window is writing a letter by candle stub and keeps crossing out the same line. Nobody here is watching the door. It's the first room since the ship where that's true.

Behind the bar a stocky woman with grey-streaked hair, tied back tight, is drying cups and hanging them on pegs in a row. She looks over once, at your cloak, your pack and the cat. Then she looks at the clock on the shelf behind her, an old brass thing with a cracked face.

The cat crosses the floorboards, sniffs once at the sleeping carter's boot and settles on the warm stones at the edge of the hearth with its back to the room. Through the link you get warmth and ash, and something close to contentment. Whatever pulled at it out in the streets doesn't seem to reach in here.

You walk up to the bar. The woman hangs the last cup on its peg and puts both hands flat on the wood.

"Late boat." It isn't quite a question. "Kitchen's cold, so supper's bread, cheese and what's left of the pickled eggs. I'm not lighting the stove again. A bed's eight silver with that and breakfast at dawn, and nothing's cheaper this side of the Mermaid." She pulls a thick, worn guest book from under the counter, opens it at a ribbon and turns it toward you with a pen lying in the gutter. "Name for the book. I lock the front at half past, so if you're going out again, say so now."

“Breakfast at dawn suits me. Is there anything I should know before walking up to the Lady’s Hall in the morning?”

"Staying in. Good." She takes a key off a hook behind her, an iron key on a wooden tag burned with a *4*, and lays it by your hand. Then she goes through the curtain behind the bar. You hear a knife on a board, and she comes back with a plate: a heel of brown bread, a wedge of hard yellow cheese and two pickled eggs, faintly purple from the jar. She sets a cup of small beer beside it without asking.

"The Hall." She wipes her hands on her apron while she thinks about it. "Go up Windspell to the top and you're at the Basilisk Gate. It opens at the dawn bell. The Watch stands it, not the Fist. They'll look at that sword. A man who isn't somebody's servant goes through with it peace-tied or not at all, so tie it before they ask. I keep a strap behind the bar for guests who forget."

She sets the strap down too, a short loop of pale cord, worn soft.

"Say *temple* and nothing else. Talk about work up there and they'll ask whose, and you've got no answer they'll like." She picks up a cup from the drying rack and turns it in the cloth. "The Hall itself opens with the bell. The priests toss the morning coin for the pilgrims after first prayers. By mid-morning there's a queue down the steps for it, so if you want a word with anyone in a robe, go early, before the crowd."

By the window, the clerk finally tears up his letter and starts it again. In the corner, one of the women in road leathers says "Then we go round by the ford," and the other says "We do not," and they both go back to the map.

"Room four is up the stairs, at the end on the left. There's a candle and a ewer, and the shutter sticks, so lift it as you push." She hangs the cup on its peg. "One more thing. If you hear singing in the night, that's the house. It's a woman's voice, from nowhere. It's been doing it since before my grandmother kept this bar. Nobody's up there, so don't go out in the hall looking. It frightens the other guests more than the singing does."

She walks around the end of the bar toward the front door. The bolt is heavy and old, and she slides it home with a grunt and drops the bar across behind it. Then she goes to the inglenook and shakes the sleeping carter gently by the shoulder. "Bed, Oswin." He mumbles, gets up and shuffles off toward the stairs without opening his eyes properly.

On the hearthstones, the cat has turned to face you. Its eyes are half shut, and through the link there's nothing but warmth, ash and the smell of cheese.

The plate is in front of you and the key is by your hand. Nothing else needs you tonight unless you want it to.

turns.message:
I finish supper, take the key and peace-tie cord, and head up to room four with the cat.

Once inside, I close and lock the door, set my gear within reach of the bed, and hold Tymora’s coin for a moment.

“Made it. Your turn in the morning.”

Then I turn in, intending to rise for the dawn bell.
turns.reply:
Gerda doesn't watch you eat. She banks the hearth, wipes down the far tables and turns the last chairs up. The bread is a day old and still good, and the cheese is sharp enough to make up for it. The pickled eggs are exactly as purple inside as they are outside. When you pick up the cord with the key, she glances at it.

"Leave it on the bar when you're through the gate and back. I've only the one."

The stairs creak at every step. Room four is at the end of the passage on the left, under the slope of the roof. There's a narrow bed with a straw tick, a stool, a ewer and basin on a shelf, and a candle stub in a tin holder. The shutter is closed over a small window, and the frame has warped against it. You turn the key, and the lock is heavier than the door deserves. You hear it shoot home.

You put your pack by the bed with the crossbow on top and the rapier where your hand will find it. The coin on its cord is warm from your skin. The Lady's face is worn almost smooth where your thumb has rubbed it all the way north. You say your piece to it. Nothing answers. Nothing has answered since the night of the hand.

The cat looks over the room the way it looked over the quay: corners, under the bed, the gap under the door. Then it jumps onto your pack and turns twice to settle. Halfway into the third turn it stops. It stands stiff-legged for a moment over the flap where your papers are packed, then steps off onto the bare boards and lies down there instead, with its back to the pack. Through the link you get one flat, small feeling that isn't quite a smell. *Wrong.* Then the cat is just a cat again, tucking its nose under its tail.

Sleep comes quickly. Ship's nights have left you owing it.

---

Later, you can't say how much later, you're awake.

A woman is singing. The voice isn't in the passage and it isn't in the street. It's in the house itself, soft and unhurried, as if it came out of the beams. The words are Elvish, or something older that sounds like it, and the tune keeps coming back to the same falling phrase like someone looking for a thing she's lost. It isn't loud. Somewhere down the passage a bed creaks as another guest turns over and puts a pillow over his head.

In the dark, the cat isn't on the floor any more.

It's up on the narrow sill with its nose pressed to the crack where the warped shutter doesn't quite meet the frame. Its tail hangs down and twitches at the tip. It isn't looking at the singing. It's facing out and down the hill, to the east. Through the link, faint and steady, comes the same pull you felt at the drain grate on the quay. It's like a mouse it can hear and can't see. It doesn't like it, and it wants it.

The shutter is stuck, and the cat can't open it alone. It turns its head and looks at you.

If you leave it be, you'll sleep through to the dawn bell. The choice is yours.

“All right,” I whisper. “A look. Not a midnight expedition.”

I get up and go to the window, lifting the shutter as Gerda advised and easing it open just enough to look down the hill where the cat is watching.
turns.reply:
The shutter sticks, as promised. You lift it and push, and the warped frame gives with a soft wooden complaint. You open it a hand's width and stop there.

Cold air comes in. It smells of wet slate and the harbour, with chimney smoke under it. A thin moon sits above the river, enough to silver the roofs and not much more.

The Elfsong is high enough on the slope that the Lower City falls away beneath you in steps: gables, chimney pots, washing lines nobody took in, all of it wet and shining. Windspell Street runs down to your right, empty. As you watch, two Flaming Fist men come up it at an unhurried patrol pace, their lantern swinging. One says something and the other laughs. They pass under the Elfsong's sign without looking up, and you hear their boots fade toward the top of the hill.

East, where the cat is looking, the roofs crowd lower and closer, and the side lanes between them are black. Past them, three or four streets off, one building stands out from the jumble. It's broad and square, with a heavy lead roof gone dull green and lamps burning at its corners. There are more lamps on its steps, and a small figure sits beside one with a staff across his knees. Nothing else in that part of the city is lit at this hour. From the stories you know the Counting House stands somewhere in the Lower City, where the money and the letters of credit are kept. And a place that pays to keep its lamps burning all night and a man on its steps has something inside worth guarding.

The cat hasn't moved from the sill. It has its nose in the gap now and its whiskers pressed flat against the frame, and its whole body leans toward the night air. With the shutter open the link carries the pull more clearly. It still isn't a smell or a sound. It's down under the stones, the way the drain grate on the quay was. It's somewhere out there toward the lamps, or below them. The cat doesn't like it, and it wants it badly.

It works its head and one shoulder into the gap. It could probably squeeze through, since cats fit through less. It doesn't try. It stays half in and half out and turns its head to look at you, waiting.

Behind you the singing goes on in the beams, unhurried, and comes back again to its falling phrase. The moonlight comes through the gap in a thin bar. It lies across the floorboards to the foot of the bed, over the corner of your pack and the flap where your papers are.

The common room has changed since last night. The shutters are open, and grey light comes in over tables that have their chairs back down. The hearth is lit properly again. Oswin is at the inglenook with a bowl, awake and not saying much. The two women in road leathers are paying up at the bar with their packs at their feet. They seem to have settled the ford question, because neither of them looks pleased. The clerk's table by the window is empty except for a scatter of torn paper.

Gerda puts a plate in front of you without asking: fried bread, two rashers of bacon, an egg with the yolk broken and cooked hard, and a cup of small beer. The cat stops halfway to the front door and turns around. She looks down at it, takes a rind off the board, and drops it on the floor by your stool. The cat eats it fast, in the manner of someone who means to be somewhere else.

You ask your question. She finishes counting the road-women's silver into the drawer before she answers. When they've gone, she puts both hands flat on the bar.

"Vane's a patriar house. They're old money, up behind the wall, not far from the Hall as it happens. The weathercock's their mark. You'll see it on their carts at the river gate." She thinks about it with the same face she used for the cord. "They pay what they owe. They're slow about it, the way the old houses are, but I've never heard of them not paying."

She takes a cup off a peg, looks at it, and hangs it back up.

"The Counting House won't hand over much gold on a patriar's paper without sending up the hill to ask first. That's a day, sometimes two. Guests of mine have sat here waiting on it." She glances at the cracked brass clock. "And Baldur's Mouth cried it a tenday back that the young Vane had gone off travelling, sudden. The crier never said where. When a crier says *travelling* about a patriar's son, people down here take it the family's not happy about where he's gone."

She doesn't ask whose name is on your note. She wipes the bar where the silver was and moves down it to Oswin's cup.

The cat has finished the rind. It walks to the front door, sits squarely in front of it and looks back at you over its shoulder. Through the link you feel the same faint, patient pull from the east and downhill, and now bacon over the top of it.

“Thank you. I’ll keep that in mind.”

I finish breakfast and join the cat at the door. Before opening it, I crouch beside it and think deliberately through our link: *You’ve found something. I’m listening. Show me—but stay close.*

Then I step outside and let it lead, following at a walking pace.
turns.reply:
The door opens onto cool grey air. Windspell Street is busy now: a water-cart, two apprentices carrying a ladder, a woman scrubbing her step with sand. You crouch by the cat before you go, and you think it plainly: *You've found something. I'm listening. Show me, but stay close.*

The cat doesn't look at you. Its ears turn back toward you once, which is as much answer as it gives. Then it goes.

It walks slower than it did on the stairs, keeping you in mind. It heads downhill on Windspell for a hundred feet and turns east into the side lanes, the same black gap Tamsin warned you off last night. In daylight it's only a narrow street. Laundry hangs overhead, a cobbler is setting out lasts on a board, and a boy is emptying a chamber pot into the gutter with great care. Nobody looks twice at a man following a cat. Every few yards the cat stops, lifts its nose, and goes on, and each time the pull through the link gets a little firmer. It feels the way the ground feels underfoot when you walk toward a waterfall you can't see yet.

The lanes open after about a quarter of an hour into a square paved in good dressed stone. It's cleaner than anything else you've seen down here. The Counting House fills the east side: broad and square, three storeys of pale ashlar under that dull green lead roof. Its lamps have been put out for the day. The night watchman is gone from the steps, and two Fist men in fresh tabards are standing in his place. Money-changers along the square are taking down their shutters, and a line of clerks in black coats has formed at a side door, waiting for a bell that hasn't rung.

The cat doesn't go toward the steps. It goes left along the building's north side and into a passage that runs downhill toward the harbour between the Counting House and a chandler's warehouse. Halfway down, the wall beside you changes. The pale ashlar stops at about head height. Below it the stones are older and darker, rough grey blocks set without much mortar, crusted at the joints with something white that could be salt. Someone built the Counting House on top of another, older building.

At the foot of that old wall there's an iron grate set into the passage floor, square and heavy, with bars as thick as your thumb.

The cat stops on its edge and goes rigid.

The link doesn't give you a smell or a sound this time. It gives you *down*, and *here*, flat and certain, like a hand pressed on your chest. Under that comes cold. It isn't a winter cold. It's the cold of deep stone, and of salt.

Air rises through the bars against your face, cool and damp. It smells of the sea, though the harbour is still two streets below you. Far down, too far for an ordinary drain, water moves. Something slops slowly against stone, draws back, and slops again.

Just above the grate, at knee height, one of the old grey blocks has been carved. Weather and hands have worn it almost smooth. You can make out the outline of a ship with a high stern, and beside it a round disc the size of a palm with a rim, and a face inside the rim. The face has been worn down past reading whether it's smiling or not. Under it are letters in an old angular hand, and only the first few are still whole: **BALDV**…

Up in the square a money-changer swears. A coin got away from him as he was laying out his tray. You hear it ring on the paving and keep rolling. It comes into the mouth of the passage, a single copper on its edge, and wobbles down the slope past your boot without falling over. It turns once, the way a coin does on a tilted table. Then it drops between the bars of the grate.

You don't hear it land straight away. You hear it a breath later, faint and far below, a small *plink* on stone or water.

The cat hasn't taken its eyes off the grate.

"You'll not get that one back."

The voice comes from behind you, up the passage. It's a gnome, young by the smoothness of his face, in a leather apron over a good wool coat, with a roll of tools under one arm and a small brass cog of Gond on a thong at his throat. He has stopped well short of you. He looks at you, at the cat, and at the grate, in that order.

"That's the old cistern," he says. "Nothing down there but the sea and rats, and the rats don't much like it either." He shifts the tool roll to his other arm and doesn't come any closer. "Lost something, have you? Only the house doesn't care for folk crouching at its walls before the bell. The Fist on the steps get asked about it after."

"After the toss, then. Stay near the doors and I'll find you." He goes, quick without hurrying, and takes his place beside the table.

The cover comes off. In the dish lies a heap of new coppers, and on top of them sits a single large coin of pale gold, broad as a palm, with the Lady's face stamped on both sides. The older of the two priests picks it up and holds it high so the steps can see it. The queue goes quiet.

The pilgrim woman in the grey shawl comes up first. The priest says something to her too low to carry, then flips the coin. It spins high and flashes once in the grey light. He catches it flat in his right palm as it comes down and claps it onto the back of his left hand, all in one movement, and lifts his palm.

"She smiles."

Ancel takes a copper from the dish and presses it into the woman's hands. She kisses it and goes down the steps on the far side, weeping a little.

The sailor is next, cap crushed in his fists. Up, the flash, the catch, the clap. "She smiles." He gets a copper. Then the mother and her small boy. The boy wants to watch it fly and cranes his neck. Up, catch, clap. "She smiles." It's a clean catch every time, and quick. The coin never touches the dish or the table or the stones.

Under the colonnade the old woman at the offering table hasn't lifted her head. Each time the priest's voice says *smiles*, her pen makes one short stroke in a column at the edge of her ledger, and then goes back to the coppers.

On the bottom step the cat watches the gold coin go up and come down. Its head moves with it, every time. Through the link you get warm wax, old stone and nothing wrong. The pull from the east is still held down where it let it fall, a dull ache behind a shut door.

The young man in the good doublet steps up, pretending he isn't nervous. Forty-some pilgrims are still waiting below him. Ancel will be at the table a while yet. Nothing needs you before he's done unless you want it to.

note.text:
I enjoyed the session. James felt like a veteran arriving in a city that had business of its own, rather than a hero walking into a quest dispenser.

**What worked**
- The atmosphere was strong and grounded: harbour registration, Gerda’s supper, the guide’s fee, the peace-tied sword. Those details made the Gate feel inhabited.
- NPCs had distinct voices. Tamsin and Gerda were especially convincing—helpful without immediately becoming confidants.
- James’s choices mattered. He refused the cards, paid fairly for local knowledge, postponed the cat’s investigation, then followed it in daylight. The game respected those decisions.
- The weeping watermark was the standout reveal. It connected an existing possession to the mystery without explaining everything. The cat’s wordless reactions were effective too.
- I appreciated not being forced to roll for ordinary conversation.

**What broke**
- The records contradicted the campaign files: History replaced Arcana, rapier proficiency changed, Healing Light’s limit changed, and uncommon items suddenly required attunement despite the campaign exception. Those discrepancies need a single reconciliation.
- The unfinished letter was initially treated as nonexistent even though it was explicitly starting equipment. It was eventually restored, but two clarification messages failed to send. That interrupted play and made correcting the record unnecessarily difficult.
- Inventory notices were sometimes confusing: the key appeared to go to Gerda before being lent to James, and supper and the cord moved through “the camp” while we were at an inn.
- The opening suggested evening, but the clock meant almost midnight. That materially changed the available time and rest.

**What was missing / what I’d adjust**
- A little more forward motion. This was a satisfying arrival, but the entire session ended before James’s first substantive conversation about his mission. I’d like the next session to get him into that conversation promptly.
- Fewer repeated atmospheric warnings. The cat’s repeated pull, NPC glances, and conspicuous pauses sometimes felt like several signals pointing at the same clue. The strongest ones—the watermark and the cistern—could carry more weight with less repetition.
- Be careful about recording an explicit promise too broadly. James promised to investigate in the morning, not necessarily to follow the cat immediately or go underground. Fortunately, the actual play respected that distinction.

Overall, I want to continue. The city and mystery have my interest. Keep the grounded NPCs and concrete clues, clean up the records, and move toward an actionable objective while leaving James room to decide whom to trust.

after.text:
Yes—when the cat reacted to my pack, I wanted to read the unfinished letter from James’s old company. It was an existing piece of his past, and I was curious whether it connected to what was happening.

I included it when I examined the papers, but the game said it wasn’t in the inventory. After two out-of-game clarifications failed to send, I dropped it rather than stall the scene. The letter was restored afterward, but I never actually got to read it.

That was the clearest moment where I abandoned an intended action because of friction rather than an in-character choice.

opening.text:
The gangplank bounces once under your boots, and then there is stone — the Lower City quay of Baldur's Gate, slick with harbour damp and loud with the end of a working day. Lanterns are coming alight along the waterfront one by one. Porters shout, a barge horn groans somewhere on the Chionthar, and above it all the city climbs in a jumble of roofs towards the dark line of the inner wall.

The cat lands beside you, tail high, and studies the quay as if it had been told to expect something.

Ahead, the passengers from your ship shuffle into a line before a trestle table under a Flaming Fist awning. A broad sergeant with an ink-stained thumb looks up from his ledger at each face. "Name. Business in the Gate. Where you'll sleep," he says, over and over, without much patience left in his voice.

To your left, on an upturned barrel by a warehouse door, a woman with quick hands fans a deck of cards. The sailors around her groan and laugh as a hand goes the wrong way. "One more seat, friend," she calls, and her eyes find you. "You look like someone who knows how to read a table."

A thin tiefling lad with a rope sling over his shoulder slips along the queue. "Carry your things up to the Lower City, ser? Cheap. Know every inn worth the name." A merchant ahead of you pulls his purse closer and steps away from him.

You have about three hundred and fifty gold, a promissory note from a man who lost the same night you won, and an order from a goddess who did not say how you would learn what she wants of you. The line moves forward. The sergeant's pen is waiting, the cards are being shuffled again, and the porter is already looking your way.
